section_entries.label: 1. Introduction
section_entries.mathematical_role: States the sharp moment theorem, motivates the random Euler-product model, diagnoses limitations of earlier high-moment/Markov methods, and introduces multiscale direct-moment control.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: Prime blocks behave like independent Gaussian increments with decreasing later variance
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: The Euler-product heuristic models log|zeta| by independent prime phases, identifies variance one half log log T, and observes that splitting primes into ranges creates nearly independent increments whose later blocks have smaller typical size.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: A tunable RH majorant bounds log|zeta| by primes and prime squares
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: Soundararajan's majorant permits a freely chosen polynomial length and keeps the zero contribution one-sided, while the accompanying cosine mean-value proposition supplies the orthogonality needed to integrate its powers.

related_synthesis_entries.claim: Prime ranges act like independent Gaussian increments because good blocks admit truncated exponential moments and the first bad block is suppressed by an orthogonal high moment, eliminating separate large-value tail estimates.
related_synthesis_entries.limit: The zeta result is conditional on RH and relies on polynomial lengths compatible with available mean values.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The decisive redesign is to spend the available moment budget unevenly: split a long prime polynomial into scale blocks, give the later and longer blocks lower truncation degrees, and analyze the joint exponential moment. A first block that violates its expected-size regime becomes an exceptional-set certificate rather than forcing every block to be shortened.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: A Dirichlet polynomial of length T^(1/W) permits control of only O(W) moments, while a Markov bound from moments alone loses the expected large-value scale. Harper instead writes the exponential of the full real prime sum as a product over blocks, truncates each exponential according to that block's size and length, and treats points with an oversized block using a shorter upper bound and their small measure.
directed.conceptual_reading: This is adaptive multiscale decomposition: local proof budgets are matched to the cost of each scale, and failure is localized at its first occurrence. The useful intermediate object is not a tail-counting event but a directly integrable product of truncated block exponentials.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The bridge is log|zeta| -> a long prime Dirichlet polynomial -> block real parts A_j -> a positive product approximating exp(2k sum Re A_j). This representation retains joint scale behavior and makes cosine-product moment estimates applicable.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The method needs prior size control for every block on the good set and a separate quantitative argument for bad points. It gives sharp logarithmic order but does not by itself supply matching lower bounds or sharp k-dependent constants.
directed.uncertainty: The mechanism is explicit in the prose and schematic identities. Exact block thresholds and the underlying zeta upper-bound proposition lie outside this span.

supported: The span explicitly contrasts the limited moment range for a polynomial of length T^(1/W), the loss from Markov tail bounds, and the redesign using jointly treated scale blocks with unequal powers.

It also says that an oversized piece is handled with a truncated upper bound and a small-measure bad set, and that the method gives sharp upper bounds without all matching lower bounds or the predicted k-dependent constant.
inference: Describing unequal block powers as allocating a moment budget by scale is a reasonable conceptual compression.
Calling the directly integrated truncated product a more useful intermediate object than a tail event is supported by the stated change of proof strategy.
unsupported_or_imported: The claim that failure is localized at its first occurrence imports the later S(j) stopping-time construction; this introductory span mentions a bad piece but does not define first failure.
paraphrase_or_style_risk: Phrases such as adaptive multiscale decomposition and local proof budgets are interpretive labels; they are useful only when tied to the concrete length-versus-power tradeoff.
context_or_ocr_risk: Exact thresholds, block definitions, and the underlying zeta upper-bound proposition are outside this span, as the prior output notes.
missed_mechanism: The reading should retain the source's explicit distinction from Soundararajan: earlier work split into two pieces but examined them separately, whereas this method controls all blocks jointly.
revision_instructions: Remove the first-occurrence claim from this unit or label it as later-context information, and add the joint-versus-separate block comparison as the source-bounded mechanism.

section_entries.mathematical_role: Truncates exponential series on good sets, applies prime orthogonality, bounds first-bad blocks by high powers, and separately controls prime-square fluctuations.

unit_result_entry.title: Dyadic exceptional sets keep the prime-square polynomial from spoiling the sharp moment
unit_result_entry.why_material: The prime-square contribution is split into dyadic prime ranges, typical ranges sum to O(1), and a first atypical range is penalized by a very high moment on a disjoint prime set, preserving the main log^{k^2} scale.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: A first oversized block pays for itself through a high even power
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: On S(j), the first failing block is inserted at a high even power while earlier blocks remain truncatable; orthogonality then yields an exponential penalty in beta_{j+1}^{-1} log(1/beta_{j+1}) strong enough to sum over all failure levels.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: The multiscale method transfers when a family supplies a polynomial majorant and square orthogonality
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: Under GRH, quadratic-character central values have a prime majorant with a deterministic prime-square shift, while family averaging kills nonsquare products; analogous good/bad strata then give the conjecturally sharp X(log X)^{k(k+1)/2} upper bound.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The prime-square correction is controlled by a second first-failure decomposition, now across dyadic prime ranges. Typical tails contribute only O(1); when a range is atypically large, a very high even moment of that range overwhelms the crude exponential bound, and disjointness from later primes preserves factorization.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: The sum over p<=log T of a p^{-(1+2it)} prime-square term is partitioned into P_m over 2^m<p<=2^{m+1}. Sets P(m) record the last/first relevant dyadic block exceeding 2^{-m/10}. If no block fails, the total real part is O(1). Large m have super-small measure; for the remaining exceptional sets, inserting a power about 2^(3m/4) and applying the same cosine-pairing calculation produces a penalty of the form exp(-2^(3m/4)) strong enough to sum while retaining the T(log T)^{k^2} scale.
directed.conceptual_reading: This is multiscale nuisance isolation: a secondary Euler-product term is not dismissed uniformly but given its own scale-sensitive stopping rule. The first atypical dyadic component becomes both the diagnosis and the source of its penalty.
directed.representation_or_bridge: Dyadic block sums P_m bridge the prime-square polynomial to tractable high moments. Because the exceptional block and the remaining exponential use disjoint prime sets, orthogonality reassembles them independently.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The argument controls the aggregate prime-square contribution in the required integral; it does not claim pointwise smallness. Its thresholds and the cutoff separating Cauchy-Schwarz disposal from high-moment treatment are tuned to this proof.
directed.uncertainty: The good/bad decomposition and superexponential high-moment penalty are clear, but OCR damages exact dyadic exponents and floors; quantitative transplantation requires the original PDF.

supported: The prime-square sum is divided into dyadic P_m blocks; if all blocks satisfy their thresholds the total real part is O(1), while large-index exceptional sets have very small measure.

For the remaining exceptional sets the source inserts a high even power of P_m, uses disjoint prime ranges, and obtains a rapidly decaying factor sufficient to preserve the T(log T)^(k^2) bound after summation.
inference: Describing the construction as a scale-sensitive stopping rule for a nuisance Euler-product term is reasonable.
The warning that the argument gives aggregate integral control rather than pointwise smallness is correct.
unsupported_or_imported: The output repeatedly calls m the first failing dyadic block. The definition instead chooses a failing m with every larger-index block controlled, so it is the last failure in increasing m, or the first only if the scales are scanned downward.
paraphrase_or_style_risk: Diagnosis and source of its penalty is a useful analogy only after the direction of the dyadic stopping rule is stated exactly.
context_or_ocr_risk: The extracted dyadic exponents and floor operations are damaged enough to preclude exact transplantation without the scan.
revision_instructions: Replace first-failure language by last failing dyadic index, or explicitly specify a descending-scale scan; keep the threshold, high-even-moment, and disjoint-support mechanism unchanged.
